## Discussion

By reanalyzing reads that transcriptomic pipelines usually discard, we show that cutaneous HPV is active in warts and epidermodysplasia verruciformis (EV) and transcriptionally silent in healthy skin. In cSCC and actinic keratosis it appears only as a trace, which neither greater sequencing depth nor better library chemistry turns into productive infection. Prior reports of little or no transcription in cutaneous carcinoma [@arron2011; @hultin2019; @arroyomuhr2021; @vandiver2021], and a recent review reporting beta-HPV as typically transcriptionally inactive in immunocompetent patients [@bruyere2026], gain from this work the controls, denominator and defined metric they lacked: `r comma(stats$neo_n)` cSCC/AK and `r comma(stats$uns_n)` unselected-skin libraries in one pipeline, where the same assay reaches the detection floor in `r pp(stats$neo_pctfloor)`% of cSCC/AK libraries and in `r pp(stats$ctrl_pctfloor)`% of productive controls.

This result does not settle the mechanism, because all three models predict a declining viral signal along progression. Hit-and-run predicts it because ultraviolet-induced host mutations can make E6 and E7 dispensable once a tumor is established [@viarisio2018], after which the virus may be lost from the expanding clone; protective immunity because virus-positive cells face negative selection [@strickley2019; @son2025]; cis-restriction because quiescence is the viral default [@rehm2022]. A fourth consideration concerns the readout rather than a model: late transcription requires terminal differentiation [@doorbar2012], so a poorly differentiated tumor cannot run the late program regardless. Splitting the below-floor libraries by viral gene answers both that requirement and the broader objection that an oncogene-driven mechanism needs E6/E7 function rather than capsid production, since `r tr("trace_pct_nogene")`% of below-floor skin and neoplasia libraries carry no reads on any HPV gene, early or late (@suppfig-trace). Absence in established lesions does not exclude a transient earlier contribution, and risk labels for cutaneous types carry the same limitation: a cutaneous type is classified as low-risk because it is not found in tumors, which is the observation a hit-and-run virus would also produce.

The elevated beta-HPV activity Son and colleagues found in keratinocyte clones of sun-exposed skin [@son2025] does not conflict with our silent reservoir: we analyzed whole-biopsy data without selection for ultraviolet exposure, and a signal arising from small keratinocyte clones is diluted when averaged across an entire biopsy, a documented effect for cutaneous HPV [@purdie2005]. We nevertheless agree on viral presence, recovering an any-HPV read from `r pp(stats$ak_pctany)`% of AK libraries, twice the `r pp(stats$npt_pctany)`% assay background (any-HPV OR `r fo(stats$ak_or)` against unselected skin). HPV8 was absent at both the assigned and detection levels from all `r comma(rvn("n_rna_all"))` analyzed RNA libraries, which argues against persistent productive HPV8 transcription in established lesions while remaining compatible with transient, focal or latent activity.

The rare productive infections we do find in primary skin are beta-HPV, mucosal HPV16 excepted (@supptbl-cin); this constrains how the trace result should be read. Outside warts and EV, three primary-skin lesions carry unambiguous productive infection by a cutaneous type: an HPV12-productive cSCC, and one actinic keratosis and one cSCC, each coinfected with HPV96 and HPV182 at near-complete genome coverage and high depth. All three are beta types, the genus the cofactor debate concerns, and to our knowledge none has been described as productive in public RNA-seq of primary skin. Productive beta-HPV infection of primary skin is therefore possible but rare, and the silence we report in cutaneous neoplasia is not a ceiling on what beta-HPV can do in skin.

HPV positivity in only 2–3% of libraries does not contradict a viral DNA prevalence of about 90%, for three reasons. Beta-HPV DNA loads sit below one copy per 60 cells [@weissenborn2012], beneath the detection limit of bulk RNA sequencing. The tissue sources differ: skin epidemiology studies test surface swabs and plucked hairs (92% and 73% prevalence) [@rollison2019sites], which sample different material from the biopsies RNA-seq is run on. Finally, screening panels miss 229 skin types lacking reference genomes [@bzhalava2014].

The reservoir also differs from the viruses found in tumors: fewer than 5% of skin types match later cSCC [@rollison2021]. HPV2, a principal cause of common warts [@breznik2020], is the one abundant reservoir type our assay calls productive (@fig-reservoir b): assigned in `r kA("HPV2","control_productive")` of `r stats$ctrl_n` productive controls and none of the `r comma(stats$uns_n)` unselected-skin libraries.

Petabase-scale surveys establish viral presence across body sites, but a presence catalog cannot measure activity. Because such surveys rely on assembly, integrated genomes fail to assemble across the virus-host junction, and E2 integrity in the assembled contigs does not distinguish cervical carcinoma from skin (@supptbl-e2), so it does not indicate genome state.

Several limitations apply. Archival sampling is non-random, so the absolute rate of HPV transcription in healthy skin is only an estimate. Sequencing chemistry could be resolved for only `r pp(stats$chem_pct)`% of libraries, and input amount, RNA integrity and fragment selection are unrecoverable from archived metadata. Because biopsy averaging dilutes focal transcription, our productivity estimates are a conservative lower bound. Finally, tissue and diagnosis labels are programmatic and imperfect, viral typing is constrained by the reference panel, and the data are cross-sectional, so these results describe phenomenology rather than prove a mechanism.

Cutaneous HPV is therefore productive in warts and epidermodysplasia verruciformis but usually leaves only a trace, non-productive footprint in cutaneous squamous neoplasia, regardless of sequencing depth or library chemistry. This phenotype is the baseline any theory of beta-HPV in skin cancer must address. Because all major hypotheses predict it, more precise measurement of viral activity will not separate them. That requires matched DNA and RNA profiling across the precursor-to-carcinoma transition, spatial resolution of residual viral genomes relative to mutant clones and infiltrating T cells, and interventional studies.
